source_text:
τὸς ὁ Κύριος ἐν κελεύσματι, ἐν φωνῇ ἀρχαγγέλου, καὶ ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεοῦ καταβήσεται ἀπὸ οὐρανοῦ.» «Σαλπίσει γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται, ἄφθαρτοι.» –»Τοὺς γὰρ πάντας ἡμᾶς φανερωθῆναι δεῖ ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ βήματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἵνα κομίσηται ἕκαστος τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν εἴτε ἀγαθὸν, εἴτε φαῦλον.» Μεμνήμεθα τοιγαροῦν τῆς ἱερᾶς ταυτησὶ καὶ φοβερωτάτης σάλπιγγος, ὅτε καὶ εὐσημοτάτη τῶν ἁγίων ἐστὶν ἑορτὴ κλητὴ ἁγία, κλῆρον ἤδη δεχομένων τῶν ἐν ἐλπίσι καὶ λαμπρῶν ἀνδραγαθημάτων πλουσίαν ἀντέκτισιν. Ἀναγκαῖον οὖν ἡμᾶς, ταῖς περὶ τούτων ἐννοίαις ἐπὶ τὸ λίαν ἐπιεικὲς ἀναθρώσκοντας, παντὸς καταλήγειν ἔργου, παντελῶς οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖν εἰδότος, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ κατασπιλοῦν εἰωθότος. Τοῦτο γὰρ οἶμαί ἐστιν ὃ καὶ σοφῶς ἡμῖν ἔφη Παῦλος· «Ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος ἐστὶ τὸ λοιπὸν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας, ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσι, καὶ οἱ χρώμενοι τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ, ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι.»
{ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἔοικεν.
{ΚΥΡ.} Εἶτα φησὶν, ὅτι «Τῇ δεκάτῃ τοῦ μηνὸς τοῦ ἑβδόμου τούτου, ἡμέρα ἐξιλασμοῦ, κλητὴ ἁγία ἔσται ὑμῖν. Καὶ ταπεινώσετε τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν, καὶ προσάξετε ὁλοκαυτώματα τῷ Κυρίῳ. Πᾶν ἔργον οὐ ποιήσετε ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ, ἔστι γὰρ ἡμέρα ἐξιλασμοῦ αὕτη ὑμῖν, ἐξιλάσασθαι περὶ ὑμῶν ἔναντι Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑμῶν. Πᾶσα ψυχὴ, ἥτις μὴ ταπεινωθήσεται ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ, ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτῆς. Καὶ πᾶσα ψυχὴ, ἥτις ποιήσει ἔργον ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ, ἀπολεῖται ἡ ψυχὴ ἐκείνη ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτῆς. Πᾶν ἔργον λατρευτὸν οὐ ποιήσετε, νόμιμον αἰώνιον εἰς τὰς γενεὰς ὑμῶν ἐν πάσαις κατοικίαις ὑμῶν. Σάββατα σαββάτων ἔσται ὑμῖν, καὶ ταπεινώσετε τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν· ἀπὸ ἐνάτης τοῦ μηνὸς, ἀπὸ ἑσπέρας ἕως ἑσπέρας σαββατιεῖτε τὰ Σάββατα ὑμῶν.» Ταπείνωσιν καὶ νηστείαν, καὶ ὁλοκαυτωμάτων προσαγωγὴν, καὶ μὴν καὶ ἔργου παντὸς κατάληξιν ποιεῖσθαι δεῖν ἔφη, τῶν μὲν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν τὴν νέκρωσιν διὰ νηστείας ὑποτυπῶν, διὰ δὲ τῶν ὁλοκαυτωμάτων τὴν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας ἀνάθεσιν, οὐ μεμερισμένως, ἀλλ' εἰσάπαν καὶ ὁλοτελῶς. Διά τε τῆς ἀργίας, καὶ τοῦ χρῆναι παντελῶς τῶν ἔργων ἀποφοιτῶντας, ὅτι προσήκει τῶν ἐπιγείων οὐδὲν ἀποπεραίνειν ἔτι, κατασημαίνων ἀστείως. Ἢ γὰρ οὐκ οἰήσῃ δεῖν τοὺς εἰς κατάληξιν ἤδη καιρῶν διεληλακότας, καὶ τῆς ἱερᾶς τε καὶ ἐν ἐσχάτοις μεμνημένους σάλπιγγος, καὶ εἰς νοῦν ἔχοντας τὸν κριτὴν, ταύτῃτοι καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἄνω λοιπὸν ἐκκομίζοντας θησαυροὺς τῆς πνευματικῆς εὐκαρπίας τὸν πλοῦτον, κατανεκροῦν ἡδονὰς, καὶ σωματικῶν ἀμείνους ὁρᾶσθαι παθῶν, εὐωδιάζειν δὲ ἤδη Θεῷ τῆς ἐπιεικείας τοὺς τρόπους, ἰέναι τε ἤδη μακρὰν, καὶ ἀπονοσφίζεσθαι φιλεῖν τῶν εἰς ματαιότητα σπουδασμάτων; Εἶεν δ' ἂν, οἶμαι, ταυτὶ, τὰ ἐν τῷδε τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ ὁ πονηρὸς τοῦ βίου περισπασμός.
{ΠΑΛΛ.} Οἰήσομαι· πῶς γὰρ οὔ;
pass_a_gloss: (as the divine Paul says,) 'The Lord himself in a command, in a voice of an archangel, and in a trumpet of God will come down from heaven.' 'For he will trumpet', he says, 'and the dead will be raised incorruptible.' 'For it is necessary that all of us be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things through the body toward what he did, whether good or base.' Let us remember then this holy and most fearful trumpet, when also there is the most notable feast of the saints, called holy, those in hopes receiving already as a lot a rich repayment of splendid brave deeds. It is necessary then that we, leaping up by the thoughts about these things to the very reasonable (good), cease from every work which knows to profit altogether nothing, but rather is accustomed also to stain. For this I think is what Paul also said to us wisely: 'The time is contracted for the rest, so that also those having wives be as not having, and those using this world as not using it to the full.' PALL.: It seems. CYR.: Then he says that 'On the tenth of this seventh month, a day of propitiation, called holy it will be for you. And you will humble your souls, and bring whole burnt offerings to the Lord. Every work you will not do on this very day, for it is a day of propitiation for you, to propitiate concerning you before the Lord your God. Every soul which will not be humbled on this very day will be utterly destroyed from its people. And every soul which will do a work on this very day, that soul will perish from its people. Every work of service you will not do, lasting ordinance into your generations in all your dwellings. Sabbaths of sabbaths it will be for you, and you will humble your souls; from the ninth of the month, from evening till evening you will keep sabbath your sabbaths.' Humbling and fasting and bringing of whole burnt offerings, and indeed also ceasing of every work he said must be made, outlining through fasting the deadening of the fleshly desires, and through the whole burnt offerings the dedication into a smell of sweet savor, not partly but wholly and entirely, and through the idleness and the need to depart altogether from the works, indicating wittily that it befits to accomplish nothing of the earthly things any longer. For will you not suppose it necessary that those already having driven through into the ceasing of times, and remembering the holy and at-the-last trumpet, and having in mind the judge, and therefore carrying out into the treasuries above for the rest the wealth of the spiritual good crop, deaden pleasures, and be seen better than bodily passions, and make fragrant to God already the ways of reasonableness, and go far already, and be wont to separate themselves from pursuits into vanity? And these would be, I think, the things in this world, and the wicked distraction of life. PALL.: I will suppose; for how not?
pass_b_english: Cyril: …‘The Lord himself will come down from heaven with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God’ (1 Thessalonians 4:16). ‘For the trumpet will sound,’ it says, ‘and the dead will be raised incorruptible’ (1 Corinthians 15:52). ‘For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what was done through the body, in keeping with what he has done, whether good or bad’ (2 Corinthians 5:10). Let us remember, then, this holy and most fearful trumpet, when the most glorious feast of the saints also comes, a holy assembly, as those who lived in hope at last receive as their lot a rich repayment for their splendid deeds of valor. We must therefore, rising through our thoughts on these things to great goodness, cease from every work that is known to profit nothing at all, or rather to stain. For this, I think, is what Paul too said wisely to us: ‘The time has been shortened from now on, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who use this world as though not misusing it’ (1 Corinthians 7:29, 31).

Cyril: Then it says: ‘On the tenth of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement; it shall be a holy assembly for you. And you shall humble your souls and offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord. You shall do no work on this very day, for it is a Day of Atonement for you, to make atonement for you before the Lord your God. Every soul that is not humbled on this very day shall be destroyed from its people. And every soul that does any work on this very day, that soul shall perish from its people. You shall do no work of service; it is a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations, in all your dwellings. It shall be a sabbath of sabbaths for you, and you shall humble your souls; from the ninth of the month, from evening to evening, you shall keep your sabbaths’ (Leviticus 23:27–32).

He said that there must be humbling and fasting, the offering of whole burnt offerings, and also a ceasing from every work. By the fasting he sketched the putting to death of the desires of the flesh; by the whole burnt offerings, our dedication as a fragrant odor, not in part but entirely and completely; and by the rest, and the command to withdraw wholly from works, he signified, aptly, that it is fitting to accomplish nothing earthly any longer. Or will you not think that those who have already come through to the close of the ages, who remember the holy trumpet at the last, who keep the judge in mind, and who for this reason are carrying the wealth of their spiritual harvest into the treasuries above from now on, must put pleasures to death and be seen to be above the passions of the body, must now make the ways of goodness fragrant to God, and must go far off and make it their habit to separate themselves from pursuits that end in vanity? These would be, I think, the things in this world, and the wicked distraction of life.
Palladius: I shall think so; how could I not?

choices.why: τὸ ἐπιεικές here is the virtue Cyril later calls 'the ways of goodness' (τῆς ἐπιεικείας τοὺς τρόπους).
